foliage: Circular spots with dark brown margins and tan to gray centers
Narrow yellow halo often surrounds leaf lesions
Severe infections cause leaf yellowing, browning, wilting, and defoliation

disease_cycle: The fungus overwinters on infected tomato debris or debris of solanaceous weeds
It can also survive on equipment like plant stakes and cages
Conidia are spread by splashing water from rain or sprinkler irrigation
High relative humidity, high temperatures, and prolonged leaf wetness favor disease development

cultural: Rotate crops for at least 1–2 years to non-solanaceous crops
Control susceptible weeds such as horsenettle
Remove and destroy crop debris (burn or bury infested plants where allowed)
Staking or trellising plants to improve air circulation and reduce foliage-soil contact
Increase spacing between plants and avoid overmulching to reduce humidity
Monitor irrigation to prevent prolonged leaf wetness
Use resistant tomato varieties where available
chemical: Apply registered protective fungicide sprays at regular intervals
Fungicides with active ingredients such as chlorothalonil or ethylene bisdithiocarbamate (EBDC) are effective
Common trade names include Daconil, Mancozeb, Fungonil
Reapply frequently (typically every 7 days) as per label instructions
Preventive applications of copper-based or chlorothalonil fungicides may be warranted in areas with chronic infection

notes: Preventive measures are more effective than attempting to cure infected plants
Conidia survive on both plant debris and equipment, so sanitation is critical
Excessive wetting or high humidity exacerbates disease spread
references: University of Wisconsin Plant Disease Diagnostics Clinic (PDDC). Septoria leaf spot factsheet.
Brannen, P. & Sugar, D. 2020. Tomato Leaf Spot Management in Home Gardens. University of Georgia Extension.
Jones, J.B., et al. 2014. Compendium of Tomato Diseases and Pests, 2nd Edition. APS Press.
